title: New MMA league adds old-school twist: Champ fights twice in same night
content:
An upstart mixed martial arts promotion planning a single-elimination tournament with 32 fighters next year is hoping to draw fans with a throwback proposition: having the semifinal winners fight again the same night for the championship.

Ki MMA, a venture led by the combat sports veteran Scott Coker that announced its name and basic format Monday, plans to use a variation of a feature used widely in the 1990s, one that Coker himself used in two previous combat sports operations.

The tournament, which is in its early stages of planning and which Ki MMA hopes to launch in early 2027, would divide 32 male fighters from the 145-pound class into four clusters based in different continents: North and South America, Asia and Europe. Each cluster would hold three events to whittle down to continental champions, then those four fighters would compete in one night to determine the league-wide winner.

Coker said he expects experienced fans to appreciate the format because more specialized martial arts like jujitsu require multiple fights in the same night. “Yes, it will be hard, but that’s why we did it, because we want this to be a hard gantlet to go through,” he said.

It’s a demanding proposition and, nearly 30 years later, far less common in a sport that requires intense concentrations of energy, with fighters often spending months preparing for a single bout. In the fight game, substitute opponents are often unwelcome curveballs and exhaustion is both common and expected after the focus of a big bout.

A second opponent on the same night is quite a wrinkle.

“I’ve never done it but it would be hard,” said Tyrone Woodley, the former UFC champion at 170 pounds. “Unless you went and got a submission, I think guys would change the way they train and fight.”

The Ultimate Fighting Championship built up its early lore with tournaments in which all the fights happened on the same night. Royce Gracie famously romped through the competition at UFC 1 in 1993 — three fights and three choke-outs in about five minutes combined — because his strike-happy opponents were completely stymied by defending a jujitsu master.

The UFC stopped asking fighters to compete multiple times in the same night after a card in 1999, as it spread to more jurisdictions and gained credibility with regulators in more U.S. states. Two previous organizations led by Coker, Bellator and Strikeforce, held four-fighter tournaments more recently before they were sold. So has the Professional Fighters League, which bought Bellator in 2023.

Ki MMA, which is named for a Japanese term used often in martial arts to describe inner life force and energy, does not yet have set dates or jurisdictions for its competitions. Part of that is about television: It has $60 million in initial funding but does not yet have a media rights deal.

For that, Ki has brought on Jon Rosen, a former William Morris Endeavor senior partner who in 2024 launched his own firm, Envisionary Management. Rosen is expected to lead Ki’s negotiations for television rights and to join its advisory board, said a company official who spoke on condition of anonymity because the agreement had not been announced.

The format outlined by Ki on Monday night would require at least 13 events, three in each continental cluster plus the championship. At a reveal event in Manhattan, executives mused about competitions in Japan, Korea, Brazil, Italy, France, Ireland and Coker’s hometown of San Jose, Calif.

Rich Chou, the top matchmaker for Ki, said part of the challenge would be finding unifying rules while holding events across the world with different regulatory requirements.

“We have to find a way for it all to collectively tie in because I think consistency is key for the tournament,” said Chou, the promotion’s executive vice president for athlete relations.

But there is a blueprint in the formats used by Bellator and Strikeforce, and Chou said Ki’s team had experience getting the regulations approved in California. Ki picked the 145-pound featherweight class because of its relative depth, and Chou said getting 32 fighters into a bracket requires a deeper pool, perhaps 50 fighters, to have alternates.

Coker added the format for the tournament is expected to be two five-minute rounds for the semifinal and three five-minute rounds for the final. That would be 25 minutes total fighting, the same duration as a UFC championship fight, even if it uses a very different split.

Woodley, who has lost three times in boxing since his last MMA fight in 2021, said he would quickly go for takedowns if he had to fight twice in one night.

“I think more guys are going to look for rear naked chokes and be more aggressive so they can save their body and be fresh,” he said. “Nobody wants a long, decision fight and then their body all beat up and have to give it up.”
